title: The Master of Disguise
full_review:
Dana Carvey should consider borrowing some of the masks he uses in his dreadfully dull comedy "The Master of Disguise" (Columbia). He may need them to hide his embarrassed face after his well-intentioned but misfired film hits the theaters.

Without a doubt, the slapstick humor and unsophisticated plot is aimed at tickling kids' funny bones. Comical (the word is used loosely) lines are given time to sink in and often repeated in case the audience missed them. The whole movie turns on Carvey's uninspired mimicking abilities. Yet "The Master of Disguise" drags its feet with unfunny skits and an agonizingly slow and lifeless plot that makes the film's 80 or so minutes feel interminable.

Carvey plays Pistachio Disguisey, the last in a long line of (you guessed it) masters of disguise. Pistachio, who inexplicably speaks with an Italian accent, is a friendly waiter in his father Frabbrizio's (James Brolin) Italian restaurant (located in a mock Little Italy).

It is only when the dastardly Devlin Bowman (Brent Spiner) kidnaps his mother (Edie McClurg) and father does Pistachio learn of his true destiny as a skillful camouflage artist. Devlin plans to steal the world's most precious treasures by forcing Frabbrizio to impersonate famous people (such as Jessica Simpson, Bo Derek, Jesse Ventura and Olympic sprinter Michael Johnson, who cameo in the film) and pinch items such as the Declaration of Independence and the Liberty Bell. But since Pistachio is so inept (which is supposed to be an endearing quality but is just annoying), his grandfather (Harold Gould) comes back to train in him the art of concealment. He also hires a curvy assistant for him, Jennifer (Jennifer Esposito), whose savvy helps Pistachio find his way out of a paper bag and save his parents.

Puerile jokes about the abundance of women's bottoms is out of place in this film, yet Carvey, who co-wrote the screenplay with Harris Goldberg, returns to it several times. It's not funny, so it seems pointless to even include it, especially when the film is aimed at a younger audience.

"The Master of Disguise" is likely to disappear from theaters without many people even noticing it came.

Due to some crass expressions and humor with sporadic slapstick violence, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.
(
2002
)
